query: Which material can be used for Temperature-dependent plastic deformation behaviors, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) exhibits robust temperature-dependent plastic deformation due to its unique microstructure and lattice distortions.
generation.material_initial_state: An SLM-built equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA with fine grain sizes, a distorted lattice structure, pre-existing dislocation networks, and nano-sized oxides.
generation.intervention: Exposure to elevated temperatures (up to approximately 700–800 °C) during mechanical testing.
generation.conditions: Deformation tests performed at room temperature and high temperatures under controlled strain rate conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The random distribution of multiple metallic elements causes severe lattice distortion and a wide variety of interatomic distances, fostering the formation of dislocation networks and nano-oxides.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, grain boundary strengthening and matrix hardening dominate; at elevated temperatures, although these contributions decrease due to thermal activation, sustained high-temperature plastic deformation is maintained by dislocation forest hardening and nano-oxide strengthening mechanisms.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA is expected to maintain higher yield strength and ductility at elevated temperatures compared to conventional alloys, attributed to its unique plastic deformation mechanisms which shift from grain boundary/matrix contributions to dislocation network reinforcement as temperature increases.
generation.baseline: Comparative performance with conventional high-temperature materials (e.g., Ti-48Al-2Cr-2Nb gamma alloys and oxide dispersion strengthened steels) that typically show lower strength at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis specifically applies to equiatomic HEAs produced via selective laser melting (SLM); variations in composition or processing might yield different temperature-dependent behaviors.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of the dislocation network, grain boundary reinforcement, and nano-oxide strengthening at each temperature range remain to be delineated with further experimental data.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of SLM-built equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA and subject them to standardized mechanical deformation tests across a temperature gradient from room temperature up to 800 °C. Analyze yield strength, ductility, and deformation mechanisms using microstructural characterization methods (e.g., TEM for dislocation density and nano-oxide distribution) before and after high-temperature deformation.
measurements: Grain size and phase composition (via TEM/SEM/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the HEA does not maintain high yield strength and ductility at elevated temperatures (i.e., yields a performance inferior to or similar to conventional high-temperature materials) or if microstructural analyses do not evidence the expected dislocation network and nano-oxide strengthening mechanisms.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

SLM-built equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA has relatively superior mechanical properties compared to known materials manufactured with conventional manufacturing processes and additive manufacturing processes [36] – [41] , [61] , [62] . In addition, when comparing mechanical properties with EBM-built Ti-48Al-2Cr-2Nb gamma alloy, which is attracting great attention as a high temperature material, SLM-built HEA showed higher yield strength up to ~800 °C [69] . Furthermore, when compared to oxide dispersion strengthened steels, which are developed by cryo-milling, SLM-built HEA represented excellent high-temperature strength at temperatures greater than 700 °C [70] . In our previous study, it is confirmed that the outstanding room temperature mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA can be attributed to fine grain sizes, dislocation networks and nano-sized oxides, and based on this, the authors presented their interpretation of a multiple strengthening mechanism [33] .
